name: The Golden Whip of Genghis Khan
powers: Said to rally and reward warriors of the khan
description: The golden whip of Genghis Khan is the legendary whip that the great conqueror is said to have carried and brandished to rally and reward his warriors, and in some tellings the source of his military genius. One of the most retold stories claims that Genghis Khan rode with a whip made of gold that he used to command his armies, and that its mere sight could turn a retreat into a charge. No such whip survives, and the Secret History of the Mongols does not name it; the golden whip appears instead in later heroic retellings and in the popular narrative that grew around the conqueror's rise. The object is thus best understood as a modern legend rather than a documented relic, and its currency reflects the way Genghis Khan has been reimagined as a national and pan-Asian hero. The golden whip nevertheless appears in monuments and museums, and it stands for the charismatic authority by which the steppe armies were held together.

name: The Whistling Arrow
powers: Signal whistle that directed cavalry maneuvers
description: The whistling arrow is the signal arrow of the Mongol armies, tipped with a drilled bone or wooden head that shrieked in flight, and it was used by Genghis Khan's cavalry to direct charges, ambushes, and encirclements across the steppe. Described by Persian chroniclers such as Juvaini and by Chinese observers, the arrow worked by sound rather than by wounding: the drilled head, often globular with holes, screamed as it flew, and the direction and number of whistles could carry simple commands to units spread across the plain. The technology descended from the signal arrows of the earlier steppe peoples, and it allowed the tightly coordinated movements that made the Mongol armies so formidable. The whistle is also associated with hunting and with the signals of the ordo, the ruler's camp. The whistling arrow survives as a motif of the swift, coordinated warfare that built the empire, and reproductions are made for museums and festivals.
source: Persian and Chinese chronicles of the Mongol campaigns

name: Morin Khuur
powers: Voice of the horse and the steppe
description: The morin khuur, the horse-head fiddle, is the two-stringed instrument of Mongolia whose scroll is carved as a horse's head, whose strings and bow are of horsehair, and whose sound is held to imitate the breath and song of the horse. The classic origin legend tells of a herdsman whose beloved horse was killed by a treacherous lord; from the horse's skull, skin, mane, and tail the man made the first fiddle, so that the animal's spirit would sing on. The instrument carries a deep spiritual charge: it is played in homes, at ceremonies, and at the Naadam festival, and traditional players observed taboos in its presence, regarding it as a living being. In the twentieth century the morin khuur was adopted as the national instrument of Mongolia and inscribed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. Its two strings are often described as the two poles of Mongol identity, and the instrument is taught, collected, and displayed as the emblem of Mongolian national culture.

name: Tsagaan Tug
powers: Ensign of khanly authority and national unity
description: The tsagaan tug, the white standard, is the ensign of Genghis Khan's lineage that Mongol tradition honours as the sacred symbol of the khagan's authority, kept at the mausoleum complex in Ordos and paraded at the Naadam festival together with the nine black banners. The standard is a spear shaft crowned with a horsehair tuft or a looped top, and its white colour links it to the heavenly realm, the midday sun, and peace, while the nine black standards of the great khan stood for war and the nine tribes of the Mongols. In Mongol belief the tug is an object of reverence in its own right, and the ceremony of raising and lowering it is attended by ritual and by the offering of airag, fermented mare's milk. The white standard is central to the cult of Genghis Khan that survives among the Ordos Mongols, who preserve his relics in the mausoleum. The tug remains the emblem of the steppe khans and of Mongolian sovereignty.
